findings.matters: A mid-year capital delivery rate of 49% with £8.441m reprofiled into future years shows how far delivery is running behind the approved programme, which is the same comparison a peer or lender would make.

findings.matters: A council forecasting its General Fund balance to rise while also drawing down £8.0m for an overspend is showing a reserves position a peer or lender can compare directly.

findings.headline: SEND Reform Plan accepted by government, with a High Needs Stability Grant totalling £145m due November 2026, leaving a balance of £3.7m to be funded from the reserve set up to support the Safety Valve programme.
findings.detail: The paper says the plan's acceptance is a key milestone in securing a 90% write-off of the cumulative DSG overspend. It notes that the grant will return during the later stages of 2026/27 and 2027/28, and that the reserve would also be used if government does not fully fund future deficit write-offs.
findings.matters: A government-accepted SEND reform plan with a 90% write-off tied to it is the mechanism other councils with high-needs deficits are waiting on, and the balance left for the council's own reserve is the number a finance director would check.
findings.figures: £145m High Needs Stability Grant due November 2026; £3.7m balance from reserve; 90% write-off of cumulative DSG overspend
findings.quote: Stability Grant totalling £145m due November 2026.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit is £148.7m at 31 March 2026, and the DSG is forecast to overspend by £74.3m in 2026/27.
findings.detail: The paper states that the deficit is kept off the General Fund under a statutory override, which it says was extended from March 2026 to March 2028. It also says the cumulative deficit is forecast to be approximately £150m by 31 March 2028, and the carrying cost of the deficit is circa £6m in interest foregone.
findings.matters: A large DSG deficit held off balance sheet under a statutory override is a live question for every council with a high-needs deficit, and the cash and interest cost stated here shows what the override does and does not cover.
findings.figures: £148.7m cumulative deficit at 31 March 2026; £74.3m forecast 2026/27 DSG overspend; approximately £150m forecast by 31 March 2028; circa £6m interest foregone
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, cumulative DSG deficit is £148.7m.

findings.detail: The paper notes that SEND transport expenditure has risen in recent years and is forecast at £22,253k for 2026/27, a 10% increase. It says 2025/26 had the lowest increase in recent history, which it attributes to market stability and efficiency work by Dorset Travel.
findings.matters: SEND transport is one of the most volatile costs in council budgets, so a September contract reset landing below budget is a reportable result for a peer or lender tracking the same pressure.

findings.detail: The paper says the MRP reduction of £3.1m follows the policy revision at the end of 2024/25. In the same section, interest payable on the capital programme has risen by £3.1m to reflect expected borrowing costs for the existing and new programme.
findings.matters: The MRP change offsets a rise in interest cost of the same size, so a finance director comparing their own MRP policy with Dorset's will see how one policy change interacts with borrowing costs.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: Children's Services growth is modelled at £15.4m, taking the budget to £120.5m, a 15% uplift.
findings.detail: The paper says the primary driver of the growth is the Children in Care population. It lists the Council's plans to reduce the number of children in care, shift placement mix towards local provision and reduce reliance on external providers. The paper also flags SEN pressures and grant formula uncertainty.
findings.matters: Children in care placement cost is a common driver of budget growth across English councils, and the paper sets out the specific levers it is using to influence it.
findings.figures: Growth £15.4m; budget £120.5m; 15% uplift

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: LG Futures modelling indicates a £6m reduction in grants over the multiyear settlement, 2026/27 to 2028/29.
findings.detail: The paper cites August 2026 modelling by LG Futures, which it says shows a £6m fall in grants across the multiyear settlement. The paper says this is why all new funding for Dorset relies on local decisions. Table 1 shows grants of £110.6m in 2026/27 falling to £104.3m in 2028/29.
findings.matters: The paper says Dorset did not benefit from Fair Funding 2.0 as much as some other authorities, which is a direct comparison point for finance officers facing the same formula change.
findings.figures: Grant reduction £6m over 2026/27 to 2028/29; grants £110.6m (2026/27) and £104.3m (2028/29)
findings.quote: modelling provided by LG Futures indicates a £6m reduction in grants over the multiyear LGFS (2026/27 to 2028/29).

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: Council Tax provides 93% of the 2026/27 increase in Core Spending Power, rather than new Government funding.
findings.detail: The paper says the Council's planning assumption is that it will need to use the maximum Council Tax flexibilities, currently a 3% increase alongside a 2% Adult Social Care Precept. It says that for Dorset, the increase in Core Spending Power comes mainly from Council Tax. Council Tax is forecast to rise from 68.1% of resources in 2026/27 to 72.9% in 2030/31.
findings.matters: A council whose funding growth depends on local tax decisions has less scope to respond to government funding changes, which is a point other councils relying on Council Tax growth will recognise.
findings.figures: 93% of 2026/27 Core Spending Power increase from Council Tax; Council Tax share of resources 68.1% (2026/27) rising to 72.9% (2030/31)
findings.quote: For Dorset, 93% of the 2026/27 increase in Core Spending Power was attributable to additional Council Tax income rather than new Government funding.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The revised 2026/27 capital programme is approximately £106m, with £52m spent and committed at Quarter 2, or 49% of the annual budget.
findings.detail: The paper says the capital programme was right-sized in a review approved by Cabinet in June 2026. It says the programme is progressing broadly in line with budget at the halfway point. Delivery is monitored monthly by the Capital Strategy & Asset Management Group.
findings.matters: Spend at the halfway point against a right-sized programme is the measure a finance director uses to judge whether a capital review has produced a deliverable plan.
findings.figures: Revised capital programme approximately £106m; expenditure and commitments £52m; 49% of annual budget
findings.quote: The Quarter 2 Budget Monitoring Report for 2026/27 shows a revised capital programme of approximately £106m, with expenditure and commitments totalling £52m, representing 49% of the annual budget.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The General Fund Balance is forecast to rise from £35.9m at the end of 2025/26 to £40.7m.
findings.detail: The paper says the General Fund Balance was £35.9m at the end of 2025/26 and is forecast to increase to £40.7m. The MTFP includes an annual budgeted contribution of £4.7m to the General Fund balance. The paper links the balance to the Council's capacity to manage in-year variances.
findings.matters: A rising General Fund balance is a direct measure of the council's capacity to absorb in-year variances, and it is the figure reviewed in the Section 25 assessment of reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance £35.9m (end 2025/26), forecast £40.7m; annual budgeted contribution £4.7m
findings.quote: The General Fund Balance at the end of 2025/26 was £35.9m and is forecast to increase to £40.7m.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: Total reserves are forecast to be in the region of £161m at 31 March 2027, before the 2026/27 reserve requirements.
findings.detail: The paper reports total reserves of £162.999m at 31/03/2026 and forecasts £161.170m at 31/03/2027 in Appendix 02. Earmarked reserves are forecast to fall from £127.016m to £120.413m over the same period. The paper says the £161m figure is before the use of reserves for the 2026/27 overspend, transformation and ERP implementation.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the trajectory of total and earmarked reserves against their own, and the paper ties the decline to specific calls on reserves.
findings.quote: Therefore, the total available reserves is forecast to be in the region of £161m by 31 March 2027.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The paper says the Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit is projected to return to around £150m at 31 March 2028, after receiving a £145m grant.
findings.detail: The paper says the SEND Reform plan was accepted in October 2026 and that the High Needs Stability grant is expected in November. It says that the statutory override ceases at 31 March 2028. It also says that if the override ends without a full write-off, many Section 151 officers across England would be considering a section 114 notice.
findings.matters: A projected DSG deficit returning above £150m when the statutory override ends is the single largest risk the paper identifies for reserves, and the same mechanism applies to every council with a DSG deficit.
findings.figures: Grant £145m; cumulative DSG overspend around £150m at 31 March 2028
findings.quote: Despite receiving £145m grant the SEND reform plan projections indicated a cumulative DSG returning to an overspend of around £150m at the 31 March 2028, when the statutory override ceases.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The Section 151 officer has assessed the current financial risk level as high.
findings.detail: The paper states that the Section 151 officer has assessed the current financial risk as high, taking into account local and national context. It says that continuing to set and deliver a balanced budget will require reprioritisation of service delivery. The paper also records the risk assessment as Capacity (High) at this stage.
findings.matters: A Section 151 officer's own risk rating is the view a lender or auditor will weigh most heavily when reading the council's budget resilience.
findings.quote: has assessed the current financial risk level as high.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: Total savings identified to date are £9.67m, against £56.76m of service budget pressures for 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper states that total pressures within service budgets are £56m and total savings identified to date are £9.67m. Savings are concentrated in Adult Social Care at £5.65m and Economy & Environment at £4.02m. Children's Services and Core Services show no savings in the table.
findings.matters: The ratio of identified savings to pressures is the figure a finance director would use to judge how much of the gap is covered by named actions rather than assumptions.
findings.figures: Total pressures £56.76m; total savings £9.67m; Adult Social Care savings £5.65m; Economy & Environment savings £4.02m
findings.quote: Total savings identified to date £9.67m

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The 2027/28 budget gap is £36m, up from £17.6m reported in February 2026.
findings.detail: The paper reconciles the rise in the gap using a table of changes. Funding adjustments add £2.7m, other changes (interest, capital and increments) add £5.1m, and directorate pressures and savings add £10.6m. The paper says the Council would need to identify £36 million of savings to avoid drawing on reserves to balance 2027/28.
findings.matters: A widening gap between February and October is a useful benchmark for peers and lenders tracking how quickly the budget position moves within a single planning cycle.
findings.figures: Budget gap £17.6m (Feb 2026) to £36.0m (Oct 2026); funding adjustments £2.7m; other changes £5.1m; directorate pressures and savings £10.6m
findings.quote: reconciles the increase from a net budget gap of £17.6m to £36m.

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The paper states that savings targets for 2026/27 are not on track to be achieved.
findings.detail: Alongside the £8m forecast overspend, the paper says that savings targets are not on track. It also says the sustainability of short-term or non-recurrent savings made this year to manage the 2026/27 position must be reviewed.
findings.matters: Savings slippage in the current year carries into the base budget, which is the mechanism by which an in-year overspend becomes a multi-year gap.
findings.quote: savings targets not being on track to be achieved

findings.paper_title: 2026-11-10 MTFP and budget report to Cabinet
findings.headline: The Quarter 2 2026/27 forecast overspend for the current year is £8m.
findings.detail: The paper reports a Quarter 2 forecast overspend of £8m for 2026/27. It says the forecast has been refined over the summer with additional pressures built in. The paper states that an overspend in the current year affects the base budget for future years if required savings are not delivered in time.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council will want to compare how this £8m is being met, from reserves or contingency, against their own in-year position.
findings.figures: £8m forecast overspend for 2026/27
findings.quote: The Quarter 2 2026/27 financial management report to Cabinet sets out a forecast overspend for the current year of £8m.

findings.headline: Dorset Council says disposal of income-generating assets may reduce its rental income
findings.detail: The paper states that disposing of income-generating assets may reduce rental income. It says disposal decisions also weigh future investment needs, maintenance and borrowing costs, and that the council is not always able to fund that investment given competing priorities.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council weighing disposals against rental income will recognise the trade-off the paper sets out.
findings.quote: The disposal of income-generating assets may result in a reduction in rental income received by the Council.

findings.headline: Dorset Council has secured approximately £50,000 from overage and easement payments since November 2025, with a further £100,000 anticipated over 12 months
findings.detail: The paper reports receipts from overage and easement agreements alongside capital disposals. Other cases are being progressed and are expected to generate £100,000, subject to agreements and trigger events.
findings.matters: Overage and easement income is a non-capital receipt source that other councils with large estates may track separately.
findings.figures: approximately £50,000 secured; £100,000 anticipated over the next 12 months
findings.quote: Since November 2025, approximately £50,000 has been secured through the receipt of overage and easement payments.

findings.headline: Dorset Council reports disposal progress 'broadly in line' with the approved pipeline timescales
findings.detail: The paper says several disposals are progressing through longer due diligence, legal and planning processes. It states that a significant proportion of sites are at exchanged or under offer stage, which it says gives confidence the anticipated capital receipt profile remains achievable. Its stage table shows 23 sites not yet started (2027 onwards) and one removed from the pipeline.
findings.matters: It shows a council reporting its receipts profile against a published timetable, with the delays and their causes stated.
findings.figures: 23 sites not yet started (2027 onwards); 1 site removed from pipeline; 9 under offer; 8 marketing or negotiating
findings.quote: Progress is broadly in line with the programme and timescales set out within the approved disposals pipeline.

findings.headline: Twelve further Dorset properties exchanged contracts, expected to generate £2.6m in capital receipts on completion over the next six to nine months
findings.detail: Twelve properties have exchanged contracts and are expected to complete over six to nine months, subject to legal and contractual process. The paper states that including exchanged properties, receipts secured and delivered are expected to exceed £6.1m, more than three times the 2024/25 total.
findings.matters: Exchanged sales give a visible forward view of receipts a finance director can build into the capital programme, and the timing is stated.
findings.figures: twelve properties exchanged; £2.6m expected on completion; six to nine months; exceed £6.1m including exchanged properties

findings.detail: The council's cash and treasury investments fell by £33m (57%) during 2025-26, from £58m to £25m. This was a deliberate strategy to offset external borrowing requirements by divesting from inherited pooled fund portfolios. The investment portfolio declined from £27.7m to £1.3m, and investment income fell to £4.9m from a budget of £6.9m as a result of both the smaller portfolio and reduced yields from interest rate cuts during the year.
findings.matters: This material reduction in liquid reserves significantly affects the council's financial flexibility and internal borrowing capacity, signalling a structural shift toward reliance on external debt and potentially constraining the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs or fund future capital investment.
findings.figures: Cash and investments £25m at 31 March 2026 versus £58m at 31 March 2025; investment holdings down from £27.7m to £1.3m; investment income £4.9m actual versus £6.9m budget
findings.quote: Cash and cash equivalents of £24m and treasury investments valued at £1m, in total £25m, down £33m from £58m at 31 March 2025

findings.headline: Council attributes overdue backlog increase to legacy audit planning with unrealistic implementation timelines
findings.detail: The council acknowledges that historical audit actions received implementation dates based on 'indicative timelines that did not always fully reflect delivery complexity, dependencies, or the time required to embed sustainable change,' contributing to the increase in overdue actions as older actions passed their original dates.
findings.matters: Peers need to understand whether a council has addressed the capacity and planning issues that led to audit action delays, as this affects future audit action delivery timelines, control environment maturity, and organizational risk management.
findings.figures: 30 overdue actions; legacy planning approach contributed to 28 actions slipping past original dates since June 2026
findings.quote: The increase should also be considered in the context of a legacy approach to audit action planning, where some implementation dates were set using indicative timelines that did not always fully reflect delivery complexity, dependencies, or the time required to embed sustainable change.

findings.headline: Overdue audit actions increased to 30 from 18 in June 2026 despite 21 actions completed in the period
findings.detail: Since June 2026, while the council completed 21 audit actions, 28 additional actions became overdue as they passed their original implementation dates, resulting in a net increase from 18 to 30 overdue actions. The council attributes this to legacy audit planning with overly optimistic timelines that underestimated delivery complexity.
findings.matters: A peer council's reversal from improving to deteriorating audit backlogs indicates control environment challenges and raises questions about audit action planning rigor and organizational capacity to deliver improvements at the pace required.
findings.figures: 30 overdue (up from 18 in June 2026), 49 total outstanding, 21 completed in period, 28 newly overdue
findings.quote: Since the previous report, a further 28 audit actions have become overdue as they have passed their original implementation dates. As a result, whilst 21 actions have been completed during the reporting period, the overall number of overdue actions has increased compared with the position reported to Committee in June.

findings.headline: Benefits management strengthened through standardised scorecard and portfolio tracker with assigned accountable officers, though dependent on resolution of data quality challenges.
findings.detail: Benefits management has matured since June 2026 with introduction of a standardised benefits scorecard and portfolio-wide benefits tracker providing greater visibility of forecast, achieved and at-risk benefits. Each saving is assigned to a named accountable officer with delivery confidence reported through the Transformation Board via fortnightly assurance reporting. However, the arrangements are dependent on critical data challenges being addressed and therefore do not eliminate delivery risk; they are described as strengthening visibility and assurance over benefits management and validation.
findings.matters: Visibility and accountability for individual benefit realisation is essential for a lender to assess whether promised savings will materialise or be deferred; strengthened tracking suggests seriousness but dependency on unresolved data issues creates lingering concern.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: A standardised benefits scorecard and portfolio-wide benefits tracker have now been introduced, providing greater visibility of forecast, achieved and at-risk benefits.

findings.headline: Governance maturity risk rating improved from high to medium between June and October 2026, as portfolio moved from design to implementation phase.
findings.detail: The council's assessment of governance maturity improved from high risk in June 2026 to medium risk in October 2026, driven by establishment of clearer senior leadership accountability, strengthened Transformation Board, maturing Design Authority arrangements, critical path reviews and more structured benefits oversight. The overall portfolio remains high risk, but the nature of risk has evolved: uncertainty regarding organisational direction and governance has reduced, with risk now increasingly concentrated on delivery, organisational capacity, benefits realisation, ERP implementation, data readiness and service stabilisation.
findings.matters: The shift from governance uncertainty to implementation risk signals the council has resolved directional questions but must now execute complex interdependent delivery; this is a material change in what can go wrong.
findings.figures: Governance maturity: High (June) to Medium (October); Strategic clarity: High (June) to Medium (October)
findings.quote: Since June 2026, governance maturity has improved through the establishment of clearer senior leadership accountability, a strengthened Transformation Board, maturing Design Authority arrangements, critical path reviews and more structured benefits oversight.

findings.headline: Data quality and records management identified as medium risk to ERP readiness, automation reliability and service continuity.
findings.detail: Poor data quality, inconsistent ownership or large volumes of outdated or unstructured information could undermine ERP readiness, automation reliability and service continuity. The council is addressing this through a project to improve information management using the Microsoft 365 platform, data migration activity within the ERP programme, and relaunch of responsibility for Heads of Service as information asset owners. This remains a material area of continuing risk.
findings.matters: A major systems implementation is only as effective as the data being migrated into it; poor data quality can cause runtime failures, incorrect financial reporting, and service disruption.
findings.figures: Risk rating: Medium
findings.quote: Poor data quality, inconsistent ownership, or large volumes of outdated or unstructured information could undermine ERP readiness, automation reliability, and service continuity.

findings.headline: Organisational capacity identified as principal constraint on transformation delivery, requiring deliberate choices about sequencing and pace of change.
findings.detail: The council identifies organisational capacity as one of the principal constraints on delivery. Multiple programmes rely upon shared leadership, operational specialists, finance, HR, digital and change resources. The council notes the principal challenge is not a lack of ideas but finite organisational capacity to deliver change. The council is making deliberate choices about sequencing and pace of change, recognising that attempting to accelerate all activity simultaneously may increase delivery risk and reduce benefits realisation.
findings.matters: If a council lacks capacity to deliver planned programmes in parallel, it risks either failure to deliver savings and benefits, or dilution of delivery quality affecting financial sustainability.
findings.figures: None provided
findings.quote: Organisational capacity remains one of the principal constraints on delivery. Multiple programmes rely upon shared leadership, operational specialists, finance, HR, digital and change resources.

findings.headline: Delivery of third-party spend reduction in 2026/27 at high risk due to limited capacity within commissioning and procurement functions.
findings.detail: The council has identified a specific high risk to delivery of third-party spend reduction in 2026/27, attributed to limited capacity within the commissioning and procurement functions. Mitigation includes additional financial oversight through recruitment of an interim deputy S151 officer, engagement with industry experts and rapid analysis, and a dedicated project team to progress contract uplift activities.
findings.matters: Third-party spend represents significant council expenditure; capacity constraints in the function managing this spend create delivery risk to planned cost reductions.
findings.figures: No target spend reduction quantum stated
findings.quote: There is a risk to delivery of third party spend reduction in 2026/27 due to limited capacity within the commissioning and procurement functions.

findings.headline: Delivery of transformation savings target in 2026/27 remains high risk, dependent on achieving timely service redesigns, workforce transitions, third-party spend reduction and accurate evidence of benefits.
findings.detail: The council assesses delivery of the transformation savings target as high risk. Success depends on multiple interdependent deliverables including timely service redesigns, successful consultation, workforce transitions, conversion of opportunities into confirmed costed savings, validated third-party spending reductions, and accurate recording of workforce changes to avoid double counting. Benefits management has been strengthened with assigned accountable officers and fortnightly Transformation Board reporting, but the overall benefits position remains high risk due to dependency across redesign activity.
findings.matters: A lender needs confidence that planned savings will materialise; high interdependency means delays or failures in one area cascade across the entire benefits realisation plan.
findings.figures: No savings target quantum stated in this report
findings.quote: Delivery of the transformation savings target remains high risk because it depends on timely redesign, consultation, workforce transition, third-party spend reduction and accurate evidence of delivered benefits.

findings.headline: ERP programme brought back under closer control due to leadership and operational concerns, with impact on delivery timetable.
findings.detail: The council identified concerns regarding the operation and leadership of the ERP programme during the period and acted to bring it back under closer organisational control with dedicated interim programme leadership and senior sponsor oversight. The council states this interruption has affected progress and is expected to impact the previously planned delivery timetable. ERP remains identified as the most significant source of residual risk within the portfolio.
findings.matters: A major systems implementation on the critical path to the council's transformation and financial sustainability has experienced leadership disruption requiring remediation, with timeline slip expected.

findings.quote: During the period, concerns were identified regarding the operation and leadership of the programme. The council acted in response, bringing the programme back under closer organisational control and putting dedicated interim programme leadership in place, with oversight from the Head of Transformation and senior sponsors. This interruption has affected progress and is expected to have an impact on the previously planned delivery timetable.

findings.detail: The auditors are undertaking additional testing of transactions processed through Commensura to address issues identified in prior years relating to the Building Health and Safety team. The paper does not specify the nature of those prior issues.

findings.matters: Asset valuations are material to balance sheet presentation; amendments at this scale indicate potential issues with valuation methodology, assumptions, or completeness that require correction in the final accounts.

findings.detail: Testing of grant income identified a material misstatement in the classification of certain social care grants. These grants are currently credited to taxation and non-specific grant income but should be credited to services due to restrictions on permitted expenditure. The misstatement affects both the current 2025/26 and prior year financial statements.
findings.matters: Material misstatements in financial statement classification are significant audit findings requiring correction in audited accounts, affecting year-on-year comparability and the accuracy of income reporting.

findings.headline: ICT recovery capability improved following resilience testing, increasing operational continuity confidence.
findings.detail: Risk 92 improved in Q1 following regular testing of resilience, recovery and service continuity arrangements. Testing demonstrated that key controls operate effectively across critical services and included previously untested scenarios. Further exercises planned.
findings.matters: Demonstrates the council has tested and validated its ability to recover from operational disruptions, reducing service continuity risk.
findings.figures: Risk 92, improved since Quarter 4

findings.detail: Risk 82 improved in Q1 through strengthened financial and procurement controls, enhanced oversight arrangements, and additional specialist capacity. findings.figures: Risk 82, improved since Quarter 4

findings.matters: Material operational and financial risk with potential to disrupt service delivery and compromise data integrity and security.

Reassurance from the Cabinet Member for Education and Finance was requested. The action remains in-progress with no completion date.

findings.detail: In-year overspends in the schools budget show a sharp upward trend over four years: £23.7m in 2023-24, £37.3m in 2024-25, £55.2m in 2025-26, and £73.7m forecast for 2026-27. Each year's overspend is substantially larger than the previous year, with the rate of acceleration itself increasing, indicating the underlying problem is worsening.
findings.matters: Accelerating year-on-year overspends indicate a structural and worsening mismatch between school funding allocations and actual costs that requires urgent intervention

findings.detail: The cumulative DSG deficit has grown substantially from opening position, despite receiving £23.75m of DfE Safety Valve funding in 2021-22 to 2022-23 and Dorset Council contributing £3.9m through Schools Block transfers. The forecast closing deficit of £221.9m by March 2027 remains at a historically high level, indicating that government and council support have not resolved the underlying structural problem.
findings.matters: A cumulative DSG deficit of this magnitude represents a significant and persistent financial pressure on the council that will constrain overall council finances and borrowing capacity

The council notes that any reforms will take time to implement and that materials from the DfE suggest staged implementation of the changes. This represents the council's response to the structural High Needs Block overspend challenge.
findings.matters: The outcome of the SEND reform process will determine whether the council has a pathway to managing the High Needs Block deficit; delayed or limited reforms could extend the funding pressure.

findings.quote: Dorset submitted their Local SEND Reform Plans in June 2026 with outcomes expected to be announced in the Autumn 2026.

findings.headline: Early Years Block funding has significantly increased due to new entitlements, creating deliverability and demand prediction risks.
findings.detail: The Early Years Block has significantly increased in funding as a result of new entitlements and changes, including extension of 15-hour entitlements to 30 hours from 1 September 2025 for working families with children from 9 months old and 2-year-olds. Risks include deliverability of the new entitlements and understanding and predicting demand. Extending entitlements for working families has made it more challenging for families of early learning 2-year-olds to secure their 15-hour weekly places.
findings.matters: Rapid expansion of early years entitlements creates both demand uncertainty and potential service delivery gaps; failed demand forecasting could create overspends in this block.
findings.figures: No current overspend reported in Early Years Block; entitlements extended to 30 hours from 1 September 2025
findings.quote: The Early Years Block has significantly increased in funding because of new entitlements and changes. Risks within the sector include deliverability of the new entitlements and (including financially) understanding and predicting the demand for the new or extended entitlements.

findings.detail: Overall surplus levels are forecast to reduce from 39 schools with £10.56m surplus in 2025-26 to 38 schools with £6.13m in 2026-27. The total value of school deficits is predicted to increase from £349,265 across 6 schools to £532,948 across 7 schools. The council is working with schools in deficit to ensure deficit reduction plans remain on track, often involving Education Challenge Leads to ensure deficit reduction does not compromise school improvement.
findings.matters: Declining school balances and increasing number of schools in financial difficulty indicates schools are facing budget pressures that may require council intervention or support.
findings.figures: 2025-26: 39 schools with £10,558,840 surplus, 6 schools with -£349,265 deficit; 2026-27: 38 schools with £6,130,463 surplus, 7 schools with -£532,948 deficit

findings.headline: Rising Education, Health & Care Plan numbers since 2014 SEND reforms are the significant driver of the historic DSG deficit.
findings.detail: The paper identifies the continued rise in the number of children and young people requiring an EHCP as a significant driver for the historic deficit. This growth has continued since the introduction of SEND reforms in 2014. However, current EHCP data as at the end of July is unavailable due to ongoing delays with reporting and data cleansing from the Synergy Case Management system implemented on 7 May 2025.
findings.matters: EHCP numbers are the key demand driver affecting the council's high needs spending and cumulative deficit position; lack of current data limits visibility of whether demand growth is continuing or slowing.

findings.quote: A significant driver for the historic deficit is the continued rise in the number of children and young people who require an Education, Health, and Care Plan (EHCP). Chart 1 demonstrates this growth since the introduction of the SEND reforms introduced in 2014.

findings.headline: Government support for future DSG deficits will be provided only on an 'appropriate and proportionate' basis and 'will not be unlimited'.
findings.detail: While government support has been significant in reducing the historic cumulative deficit, there is no guarantee that future deficits will receive the same level of support. The government has explicitly stated that assistance in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be limited. Continued High Needs Block overspends could mean the deficit reaches around £150m by March 2028 even after a 90% write-off, if future government support is more restricted.
findings.matters: Uncertainty about the extent of future government funding means the council cannot rely on current support levels continuing, creating a material funding gap risk for high needs provision.
findings.figures: 90% write-off of existing deficit mentioned; potential deficit around £150m by March 2028; support terms apply to 2026/27 and 2027/28
findings.quote: Government support would significantly reduce the current historic deficit, however there is no guarantee that future deficits will receive the same level of support, with Government stating that assistance in 2026/27 and 2027/28 will be provided only on an "appropriate and proportionate" basis and "will not be unlimited".

findings.headline: Q1 2026-27 forecast £73.737m overspend would bring cumulative DSG deficit to £221.87m by year-end.
findings.detail: The July 2026 forecast position shows a £73.737m in-year overspend for 2026-27. Adding this to the historic cumulative deficit position of £148.7m would produce a revised cumulative deficit of £221.87m. The prior year 2025-26 outturn was a £54.45m overspend, with the forecast overspend currently within the High Needs Block.
findings.matters: A significant in-year overspend that would grow the cumulative deficit by over 50% in a single year signals accelerating pressure on the high needs system and rising contingent liability.
findings.figures: £73.737m forecast overspend for 2026-27; cumulative deficit would reach £221.87m (up from £148.7m); 2025-26 outturn was £54.45m overspend
findings.quote: At the 31 July 2026, the forecast outturn is a £73.737m overspend for 2026-27 (Appendix A). Adding the historic cumulative deficit position, a revised cumulative deficit would be £221.87m.

findings.headline: Cumulative DSG deficit of £148.7m kept off council's balance sheet via statutory override extended to March 2028, but creating £4.9m annual cashflow pressure.
findings.detail: The deficit is held separately from the General Fund under The Local Authorities Capital Finance and Accounting (England) Regulations, with the override extended from March 2026 to March 2028 in June 2025. However, the £148.7m deficit means the council has access to £148.7m less cash than it would otherwise, resulting in £4.9m annual interest foregone that must be met by the General Fund and could otherwise be spent on local service delivery.
findings.matters: A material off-balance-sheet deficit affecting council cash availability and requiring General Fund subsidy is a key financial risk that lenders and peer councils monitor closely.
findings.figures: £148.7m cumulative deficit as of 31 March 2026; £4.9m annual interest foregone; statutory override extended to March 2028
findings.quote: As of 31 March 2026, cumulative DSG deficit is £148.7m. Any deficit associated with the DSG is kept off council's balance sheets because of the statutory override set out in The Local Authorities Capital Finance and Accounting (England) Regulations.
