findings.headline: Weymouth Harbour £2.6 million reserves designated for substantial infrastructure investment programme over coming years
findings.detail: Weymouth's forecast reserve balance of £2.6 million is committed to delivering a programme of works in line with the Harbour Business Plan. The report notes that over the next few years, several costly projects are scheduled, with Weymouth Harbour's extensive infrastructure being expensive to maintain and replace. These funds are required to support the forward capital plan.
findings.matters: While reserves appear healthy, they are already allocated to necessary infrastructure maintenance and replacement, meaning limited discretionary funding and forward capital pressures.
findings.figures: £2.6 million forecast reserves; multiple costly capital projects scheduled
findings.quote: The reserve balance for Weymouth is forecast to be £2.6 million.

findings.headline: Weymouth Harbour surplus forecast to increase to £675,607, significantly above the £603,300 budget
findings.detail: Weymouth is forecast to deliver a surplus £72,307 above budget, driven primarily by £157,184 favourable income variance. Despite some revenue mix challenges (marina berthing down 1.6%, visitor overnight berthing slightly below budget), strong performance in slipway usage, water sports permits, and new fuel sales income more than compensate. Car park income is also exceeding forecasts despite partial Pavilion car park closure.
findings.matters: Shows a material harbour operation outperforming expectations, generating stronger-than-budgeted revenue to support future infrastructure investment.
findings.figures: £603,300 budgeted surplus; £675,607 forecast surplus; £157,184 overall favourable income variance
findings.quote: Weymouth Harbour budget was originally set to deliver a year-end surplus of £603,300. The current forecast indicates an increase to this surplus to £675,607.

findings.headline: Lyme Regis Harbour operating with zero reserve balance and requirement to deliver a balanced budget
findings.detail: Lyme Regis has no current reserve balance and must run a cost-neutral operation. Cost pressures including additional business rates and licence income below budget must be managed to maintain the balanced budget requirement, leaving no financial buffer for unexpected costs or revenue fluctuations.
findings.matters: A revenue-generating service with zero financial headroom and no flexibility to absorb unexpected costs represents a financial vulnerability and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: £0 reserves balance; balanced budget requirement
findings.quote: Lyme Regis does not currently have a balance in reserves.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 3 - Financial Summary Weymouth (4)
findings.headline: Leisure Activities income £13,092 below budget, the only material income underperformance
findings.detail: Leisure Activities revenue is predicted at £1,152,172 against a budget of £1,165,264—an adverse variance of £13,092. This is the only significant income stream not meeting budget, alongside a minor £1,175 shortfall in Rents and Licences. All other revenue streams are meeting or exceeding targets.
findings.matters: Underperformance in a leisure revenue stream could signal demand weakness or operational challenges, relevant to financial forecasting if the trend continues.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 3 - Financial Summary Weymouth (4)
findings.headline: Operational expenditure £84,877 over budget due to cost inflation across pay, premises, parking and supplies
findings.detail: Total operational expenditure is predicted at £1,745,097 against a budget of £1,660,220—an adverse variance of £84,877 (5.1% of budget). Parking costs are £35,700 over budget, supplies and services £22,156 over, pay-related costs £16,182 over, and premises costs £10,795 over budget. These variances are more than offset by stronger income.
findings.matters: A finance director would track whether operational cost pressures are controllable and sustainable, particularly in a service relying on reserves to fund capital programs.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 3 - Financial Summary Weymouth (4)
findings.headline: Harbour reserves projected to fall from £4.14m to £2.61m in 2026/27 as service funds capital programs
findings.detail: Harbour reserves totalling £4,140,495 are projected to fall to £2,610,738 after £2,133,057 of in-year spending on capital and maintenance programs. The Development and Project reserve is drawn down by £695,000. A multi-year Walls and Floating Gates repairs program is in Year 2 of 3, with £480,000 being spent in the year from reserves designated for this work.
findings.matters: Substantial reserve drawdowns for capital programs indicate significant infrastructure investment; a multi-year repairs commitment represents a material obligation affecting the council's capital planning and reserve adequacy.
findings.figures: 4,140,495 603,300 2,133,057 2,610,738 (total reserves); Development and Project reserve drawn by 695,000; Walls and Floating Gates repairs 1,000,000 480,000 1,480,000 (Year 2 of 3)
findings.quote: Year 2 of 3: funded from reserves 1,000,000 480,000 1,480,000

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 3 - Financial Summary Weymouth (4)
findings.headline: Parking income £132,254 better than budget as Weymouth Harbour outperforms overall surplus target
findings.detail: Parking income is predicted at £697,554 against a budget of £565,300, delivering £132,254 of additional income—the largest positive variance across all income streams. Despite operational cost inflation totalling £84,877, the service is predicting a total surplus of £675,607 against the budget of £603,300, a favourable variance of £72,307. Commercial activities also outperform by £29,815.
findings.matters: A lender or finance director tracking the council's income-generating services would see this as evidence of demand resilience and revenue strength in a quasi-commercial operation.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 2 - Lyme Financial Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Lyme Regis Harbour reserve at zero with no planned transfer in 2026/27
findings.detail: The harbour reserve balance brought forward from 2025/26 is zero, with no predicted transfer to reserves in 2026/27, and a forecast year-end balance of zero.
findings.matters: A service with no reserves has no capacity to manage unexpected cost pressures or income volatility and any adverse movement would need to be absorbed by the council's general reserves.
findings.figures: Balance brought forward 0; predicted transfer to reserves 0; forecast year-end 0.
findings.quote: Balance b/f from 2025/26 0

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 2 - Lyme Financial Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Lyme Regis Harbour fees and charges forecast £1,834 below budget
findings.detail: Fee and charges income is forecast at £437,266 against a budget of £439,100, a shortfall of £1,834. The service is forecast to break even because a £7,150 underspend in pay costs offsets this income shortfall along with cost overruns in premises (£2,315) and transport (£3,000).
findings.matters: A finance director would be concerned about a service dependent on fee income that is not materializing as planned.
findings.figures: Fees and charges budgeted £439,100, forecast £437,266, variance £1,834 adverse; pay costs forecast underspend £7,150; premises forecast overspend £2,315; transport forecast overspend £3,000.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 1- Bridport Financial Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Emergency dredging for storm damage allocated at £124,000 with funding of £190,000 made available.
findings.detail: The budget monitoring paper flags emergency dredging for storm damage as a discrete spending item, forecast at £124,000 against available funding of £190,000. This indicates weather-related infrastructure damage requiring immediate action. The discretionary nature is clear from the "Emergency" label and the fact it appears separately from routine asset management.
findings.matters: Emergency infrastructure spending driven by weather damage signals climate risk exposure to port infrastructure and demonstrates that capital demands are not fully within the service's control or budget planning.
findings.figures: Emergency dredging for storm damage £124,000, with funding of £190,000 provided.
findings.quote: Emergency dredging for storm damage 124,000 190,000

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 1- Bridport Financial Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Premises costs forecast at £111,569 against budget of £48,000, an overspend of £63,569.
findings.detail: Premises-related costs are running at 132% of budget. The document does not explain the driver, but the magnitude suggests either deferred maintenance or emergency repairs. The concurrent emergency dredging spending suggests possible weather-related infrastructure damage.
findings.matters: A premises cost overspend of this scale indicates unplanned capital or major maintenance demand that the service cannot accommodate within its operating budget and will require reserve funding.
findings.figures: Premises Related Costs budgeted £48,000, forecast £111,569, adverse variance £63,569.
findings.quote: Premises Related Costs 48,000 111,569 (63,569) (A)

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 1- Bridport Financial Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Fees and charges income forecast at £751,076 against budget of £794,600, a shortfall of £43,524.
findings.detail: Harbour fee income is running 5.5% below budget. The paper provides no explanation for the shortfall, which could indicate lower than expected harbour activity, service disruption, or demand pressure. This is a material variance given that fees are the largest revenue item for the service.
findings.matters: Income volatility in a user-fee-funded service signals revenue risk to a lender and indicates whether the service is demand-dependent and potentially vulnerable to external shocks.
findings.figures: Fees and Charges budgeted £794,600, forecast £751,076, adverse variance £43,524.

findings.paper_title: Budget Monitoring App 1- Bridport Financial Summary 2026-27
findings.headline: Harbour revenue surplus forecast at £71,807 against £90,400 budgeted, an adverse variance of £18,593.
findings.detail: The shortfall in operating surplus is driven by fees and charges running £43,524 below budget (forecast £751,076 vs budget £794,600) and premises costs overrunning by £63,569 (forecast £111,569 vs budget £48,000). These are partially offset by pay cost savings of £24,000 and supplies savings of £30,000. The reduced surplus constrains the service's ability to self-fund capital and maintenance spending.
findings.matters: The revenue miss indicates the harbour is generating less cash than planned, requiring greater drawdown of reserves to fund capital and maintenance programs, reducing the council's financial flexibility.
findings.figures: Total Bridport Harbour budget £90,400, forecast £71,807, adverse variance £18,593.
findings.quote: Total Bridport Harbour 90,400 71,807 (18,593) (A)

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report
findings.headline: Family Hubs Programme Phase 1 received limited assurance, indicating control weaknesses in a new strategic initiative
findings.detail: An audit of Family Hubs Programme Phase 1 found only limited assurance with 2 Priority 2 actions. This suggests the council is implementing a new programme without adequate controls over budget, delivery or governance. The report provides no detail on the nature of the programme or budget scale.
findings.matters: New programmes with weak controls at launch create risk of budget overruns, poor delivery, or failure to achieve intended outcomes. Limited assurance in Phase 1 suggests Phase 2 implementation may face control challenges.
findings.figures: 2 Priority 2 actions; limited assurance opinion
findings.quote: Family Hubs Programme Phase 1 Final Limited 2 0 2 0 Medium

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report
findings.headline: 20 audit actions are currently overdue, up from 9 in the prior year
findings.detail: The council has 20 overdue audit actions as at 19 June 2026. Although the report notes this includes 10 Priority 3 actions now tracked (not included in prior years), the underlying trend shows persistent delays in implementing audit recommendations. The council remains at risk of actions slipping further past agreed closure dates.
findings.matters: Overdue audit actions indicate that management is not implementing agreed control improvements on schedule. Repeated action delays suggest weak accountability for remediation and increase the likelihood that identified gaps persist longer than documented.
findings.figures: 20 overdue actions as at 19 June 2026; prior year 9 Priority 1/2 overdue actions
findings.quote: Whilst the charts above show an increase in overdue actions (increasing from 9 to 20), this also includes 10 Priority 3 actions that would not have been included in last year's review.

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report
findings.headline: One Priority 1 Health and Safety action from prior-year investigation remains outstanding
findings.detail: A 2024/25 investigation into health and safety compliance resulted in 35 actions. As of the follow-up in 2025/26, three actions remain unresolved, including one Priority 1 (major concern requiring immediate corrective action). This action has been outstanding for at least 6 months since the action plan was issued in December 2025.
findings.matters: Priority 1 actions outstanding for extended periods indicate the council is not acting urgently on serious identified risks. This suggests potential gaps in management accountability and the council's ability to remediate known compliance failures.
findings.figures: 1 Priority 1 outstanding; 3 total outstanding from 35 actions; action plan issued December 2025
findings.quote: of the 35 actions identified from the investigation, only 3 are outstanding (one Priority-1 and two Priority-2).

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report
findings.headline: Governance of financial management in schools received limited assurance
findings.detail: Schools' financial management systems were audited and found to have limited control effectiveness, with 5 actions agreed (4 Priority 2, 1 Priority 3). As the council is statutorily responsible for schools' financial oversight, weak school finance controls represent a gap in the council's overall control environment.
findings.matters: The council is accountable for schools' finances. Weak school-level financial controls increase risk of misappropriation, budget overruns or reporting errors that affect the council's consolidated position and reputation.
findings.figures: 5 actions (4 Priority 2, 1 Priority 3); limited assurance opinion issued
findings.quote: Governance of Financial Management in Schools Final Limited 5 0 4 1

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council Internal Audit Annual Opinion Report
findings.headline: Data Maturity controls received limited assurance, creating potential reliability risk for financial decisions
findings.detail: An audit of data maturity governance found only limited assurance, with 10 Priority 2 actions identified. The council's data systems and governance practices are weak enough that they may not reliably support financial and strategic decision-making. The report notes that actions require time to be embedded.
findings.matters: A council's financial position and forecasts depend on reliable data. If the council's data governance is immature, there is material risk that financial reporting, reserves forecasting, and budget monitoring are less reliable than they appear.
findings.figures: 10 Priority 2 actions identified for data maturity
findings.quote: During 2025/26, three limited assurance opinions have been reported to the Committee relating to Data Maturity, Governance of Financial Management in Schools and Family Hubs Programme Phase 1

findings.headline: Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman upheld 82% of complaints compared to 85% average for similar authorities; only 11% received satisfactory remedy before escalation vs 13% average
findings.detail: Ombudsman complaint performance is worse than peer average on both metrics. Higher upheld rate (82% vs 85%) suggests complaints have merit. Lower pre-escalation remedy rate (11% vs 13%) suggests council is slower to resolve issues proactively.
findings.matters: Complaint patterns indicate governance or service quality issues not being resolved at source. Trends matter for service user confidence.
findings.figures: 82% upheld vs 85% average; 11% pre-escalation remedy vs 13% average
findings.quote: The Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman's 2025/26 report noted that 82% of complaints escalated to them and investigated were upheld, compared to an average of 85% in similar authorities.  In 11% of cases they found that the Council had provided a satisfactory remedy before the complaint reached the Ombudsman, compared to an average of 13% in similar authorities.

findings.headline: Ongoing funding pressures: underfunding from business rates distribution and limited council tax increases alongside central government settlement constraints
findings.detail: The statement notes: "Dorset Council continues to experience funding pressures through central government annual settlements, limited increases in its council tax and under funding from the current business rates distribution methodology." This is structural, not temporary.
findings.matters: Persistent structural underfunding limits financial flexibility and forces difficult savings decisions. Relevant to council's borrowing capacity and reserve position.
findings.figures: Identified as ongoing structural pressure from multiple funding sources
findings.quote: Dorset Council continues to experience funding pressures through central government annual settlements, limited increases in its council tax and under funding from the current business rates distribution methodology.

findings.headline: Chief Financial Officer transition in August 2025: Executive Director for Corporate Development was CFO until August 2025, now undertaken by Director for Finance
findings.detail: Mid-year CFO role change occurred in August 2025. No detail provided on whether this was planned, retirement, or other circumstance. Timing is late in financial year with AGS being drafted in the same period.
findings.matters: CFO transitions carry implementation risk, particularly if unplanned. Mid-year timing and proximity to audit period are material to continuity of financial control.
findings.figures: CFO transition August 2025
findings.quote: The Executive Director for Corporate Development was the Council's Chief Financial Officer until August 2025, with the role now undertaken by the Director for Finance (previously known as Corporate Director for Finance and Commercial).

findings.headline: Health service reform creates Very High risk of additional unprovisioned responsibilities and budgetary pressures with potential for unmet health needs
findings.detail: Council identifies health service reform as a Very High risk that could lead to "additional unprovisioned responsibilities, leading to increased resourcing and budgetary pressures, unmet health needs and potential harm to individuals." Response relies on lobbying and dialogue rather than budget solutions, suggesting no funding mechanism is currently in place.
findings.matters: Unprovisioned service obligations could force budget deficits or service cuts. The risk is explicitly unresolved pending new ICB structure clarity.
findings.figures: Risk rated Very High; awaiting publication of new ICB structure for clarity
findings.quote: Risk : As a result of health service reform, Dorset Council may incur additional unprovisioned responsibilities, leading to increased resourcing and budgetary pressures, unmet health needs and potential harm to individuals.

findings.headline: Investigations into Health and Safety and Contract/Expenditure Compliance found controls circumvented or absent in 2023/24 and 2024/25
findings.detail: Both 2023/24 and 2024/25 statements referenced investigations into Health and Safety Compliance and Contract/Expenditure Compliance that found controls were either circumvented or absent. The governance statement acknowledges these led to significant governance and control failings, though states that "a significant amount of work has been undertaken" to respond and internal audit review has been positive. The statement cautions that "some cultural change takes time to embed."
findings.matters: Documented control circumvention is a material governance weakness that goes to the heart of financial control reliability. Lenders need assurance that this has been genuinely remediated, not merely acknowledged.
findings.figures: Two years of AGS reporting required due to failures
findings.quote: As a result, both the Statement and annual internal audit opinions offered a limited assurance. A significant amount of work has been undertaken to respond to these findings, which are broadly complete and have been subject to positive review by SWAP Internal Audit. It is however recognised that some cultural change takes time to embed.

findings.headline: External audit identified three significant weaknesses in the 2024/25 interim report, including value for money arrangements and governance issues from Building Health and Safety investigations with ongoing police involvement
findings.detail: The interim 2024/25 external auditors report flagged three significant weaknesses: not satisfied with value for money arrangements for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness; ongoing Dedicated Schools Grant issues; and governance weaknesses due to significant findings from Building Health and Safety investigations with ongoing police investigations. These represent material audit concerns that remained unresolved at statement date.
findings.matters: External audit weakness findings directly affect lender confidence in governance and the council's ability to manage resources effectively. Ongoing police investigations indicate potential serious breaches.
findings.figures: Three significant weaknesses identified; police investigations ongoing
findings.quote: The interim 2024/25 external auditors report identified three significant weaknesses: Not satisfied that there are proper arrangements re value for money work for securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the use of resources; Arrangements for Dedicated Schools Grant (ongoing from 23/24); Governance and securing economy, efficiency and effectiveness in the use of resources due to the significant findings identified through the Building Health and Safety investigations (ongoing from 23/24).  It was noted that police investigations are ongoing.

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council and Pension Fund - Regaining Assurance Strategy July 2026
findings.headline: Auditors assess Dorset as Category A — a well-managed council capable of timely rebuild within the planned timeframe
findings.detail: Grant Thornton categorizes Dorset as 'capable of an ISA-compliant approach within the build-back period, relatively straightforward.' The council produces timely accounts with minimal audit adjustments and the finance team has sufficient capacity to support rebuild procedures.
findings.matters: This positive capacity assessment provides confidence that the rebuild plan is achievable and the three-year trajectory to unmodified opinion is credible, reducing risk of further slippage.
findings.figures: Category A classification; £145,109 Section 31 grant provided
findings.quote: Dorset is a well managed council, without significant technical and accounting challenges. We have assessed that the Council has sufficient arrangements in place to support a timely build back and assurance can be regained by 2027/28, as this aligns with the end of the scheduled property revaluation cycle.

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council and Pension Fund - Regaining Assurance Strategy July 2026
findings.headline: Another disclaimed opinion is expected for 2025/26, extending unverified accounts to a fourth consecutive year
findings.detail: Auditors expect to issue a disclaimer of opinion for 2025/26, with sign-off targeted for 30 November 2026. Audit focus is limited to in-year transactions and closing balances only; opening balances remain unverified.
findings.matters: This means four consecutive years with no audit assurance. Lenders cannot build confidence in the council's financial position; covenant monitoring is compromised.
findings.figures: Sign-off date 30 November 2026; statutory backstop 31 January 2027
findings.quote: Following disclaimed audit reports for the years 2022/23 to 2024/25, we do not expect to be able to support an unmodified opinion on the 2025/26 financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council and Pension Fund - Regaining Assurance Strategy July 2026
findings.headline: Reserve balances at 31 March 2024 remain unverified, leaving opening reserves for the current year unaudited
findings.detail: The audit assurance chart shows 'No assurance over reserve balances at 31/03/24'. Partial assurance is not expected until 2026/27 at earliest, and full assurance only by 2027/28.
findings.matters: Reserves are the primary measure of council financial resilience and liquidity. Unverified reserve balances mean the council's actual financial buffers are unknown to lenders and internal management.
findings.figures: Opening reserves for 2024/25 and 2025/26 unverified; build-back extends through 2027/28
findings.quote: No assurance over reserve balances at 31/03/24 impacting opening reserves position brought forward and closing position

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council and Pension Fund - Regaining Assurance Strategy July 2026
findings.headline: Property asset valuations are the critical audit blocker, requiring a three-year staged rebuild programme
findings.detail: Grant Thornton identifies property valuations as the key issue preventing audit sign-off. Staged asset testing is planned across 2025/26 through 2027/28, aligned to the council's rolling revaluation programme. This directly drives the trajectory from disclaimer (2025/26) to qualified (2026/27) to unmodified (2027/28).
findings.matters: Properties are typically a council's largest asset class. Inability to verify valuations prevents sign-off of the balance sheet. For lenders, uncertainty over asset values affects loan covenants and financial stability assessment.
findings.quote: Staged asset testing of property valuations across 2025/26 through to 2027/28 audits — aligned to timing of rolling valuation programme and testing of historic additions/disposals.

findings.paper_title: Dorset Council and Pension Fund - Regaining Assurance Strategy July 2026
findings.headline: Dorset Council has received disclaimed audit opinions for three consecutive years (2022/23 to 2024/25)
findings.detail: The audit opinions for years ended 31 March 2025, 2024 and 2023 were all disclaimed, meaning auditors could not obtain sufficient evidence to form any opinion whatsoever on the financial statements. This represents a complete absence of audit assurance.
findings.matters: A disclaimed opinion provides zero assurance on the council's accounts. Lenders cannot assess true financial position; the S151 officer has no external verification of reported figures.
findings.figures: Three years affected: 2022/23, 2023/24, 2024/25
findings.quote: This report sets out our plan to rebuild audit assurance at Dorset Council (the Authority) following the disclaimer of opinion issued under the statutory backstop for the years ended 31 March 2025, 31 March 2024 and 31 March 2023.

findings.headline: Overall residual risk rated High; multi-year MTFP refresh underway but 'continued focus will be required' on people services
findings.detail: Risk assessment: Current Medium, Residual High. The report attributes residual risk to 'the national picture and economic conditions affecting all local authorities' but explicitly names 'pressures continue to build in the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) for demand led service delivery to support vulnerable Adults and Children and around the High Needs Block'. MTFP refresh not due until November.
findings.matters: Forward-looking risk assessment is the council's own view of what could go wrong. High residual risk on demand-led services, combined with missed savings targets, suggests the next MTFP cycle will be difficult.
findings.figures: Residual Risk: High; Current Risk: Medium
findings.quote: The residual risk being high principally reflects the national picture and economic conditions affecting all local authorities. Pressures continue to build in the Medium-Term Financial Plan (MTFP) for demand led service delivery to support vulnerable Adults and Children and around the High Needs Block (HNB) of the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG).

findings.headline: Council tax and business rates collection both declined year-on-year; local tax base showing stress
findings.detail: Council tax collection dropped to 95.09% from 96.03%. Business rates to 95.52% from 96.36%. While cash collected increased (due to higher billings), the collection rate decline across both heads of tax suggests taxpayer stress or growing non-payment.
findings.matters: Declining collection rates signal rising hardship in the local economy and/or taxpayer base. This is a leading indicator of future revenue pressure and may constrain the council's ability to raise income.
findings.figures: Council tax 95.09% (was 96.03%); business rates 95.52% (was 96.36%)
findings.quote: The collection rate as at 31 March 2026 was 95.09%, which is slightly less than the previous year's rate 96.03%. Although the collection rate has reduced, total cash collected has increased by £30.966m

findings.headline: Capital programme slippage of £35.9m (31% of budget) carried forward; projects re-profiled significantly
findings.detail: Of £116.4m capital budget, only £75.7m was spent (65%). Major schemes re-profiled include Highways £8.34m, Local Nutrient Mitigation £3.1m, Refuse Collection Vehicles £2.5m. This suggests either planning delays or delivery risk.
findings.matters: Capital slippage that carries forward can signal delivery capacity constraints or planning risk. It also means expected asset renewal is delayed, which can increase maintenance costs later.
findings.figures: £40.6m slippage out of £116.4m budget (35%); Highways £8.34m deferred, LNM £3.1m, RCV £2.5m
findings.quote: Similar to previous years the Council has seen some programme slippage carried forward across years... There has been re-profiling of £26.6m into future years to more accurately reflect the timing of expenditure.

findings.headline: Year-end underspend depends entirely on Place, Corporate, and other services; does not prove people services are sustainable
findings.detail: Children's overspent £3.9m, Adults £5.9m, but Place underspent £7.5m and Corporate £1.6m. Without those offsets there would have been a £4.5m+ deficit. The report frames this explicitly: 'the Council's overall position depends heavily on managing the budget as one council, with some departments required to mitigate continuing demand-led overspends'.
findings.matters: This masks structural imbalance. If Place and Corporate underspends dry up (which they do in ordinary years), the people services overspends become visible. Lenders need to know whether balance is real or borrowed.
findings.figures: Total service overspend £0.532m (2024/25 was £9.995m); placement overspends offset by underspends elsewhere
findings.quote: Taken together, this shows that the Council's overall position depends heavily on managing the budget as one council, with some departments required to mitigate continuing demand-led overspends in people services.

findings.headline: Children in care and adult care demand both rising; cost-per-package also rising
findings.detail: Children in care (excluding UASC) rose 33 to 430; UASC up 3 to 44. Adult care service users up 265 to 4,536. Average weekly cost of care packages increased from £889 to £921. Externally-purchased children's homes alone overspent by £6.5m. This is structural demand growth, not one-off pressures.
findings.matters: Demand growth in high-cost services (£20k+/child in residential care) drives permanent budget additions. If demand continues to rise and unit costs keep climbing, the council cannot manage this from underspends in other departments.
findings.figures: Children in care +33; adult care users +265; average care package cost £889→£921 per week; externally-purchased homes £6.5m overspend
findings.quote: The number of children in care has risen particular in the first half of the year before broadly stabilising in the later part of the year... The adult social care budget supports approximately 4,536 people an increase of 265 people compared to the previous year (65 working-age adults and 215 aged 65+). This increase in activity has placed additional pressure on the budget.

findings.headline: Adults & Housing delivered only 77% of £10.6m savings target; Children's missed 8% of theirs
findings.detail: Adults & Housing achieved £8.125m of a £10.597m savings target, leaving £2.4m undelivered. Birth to Settled Adulthood delivered only 37% (£0.371m of £1.0m). The report acknowledges 'not all planned savings were achieved, and that some savings will need to be delivered in future years'—meaning shortfalls carry into 2026/27.
findings.matters: Missed savings targets in demand-led services signal delivery risk in transformation programmes. When savings plans don't land, councils either reduce services or pull harder on reserves. Neither is sustainable.
findings.figures: Adults & Housing 77% delivery; Birth to Settled Adulthood 37% delivery; Public Health 19% (£0.062m of £0.320m)
findings.quote: The Directorate had a savings target of £10.597m for the year. The total savings achieved in-year were £8.125m (77%). The savings target was challenging from the offset and, following a robust review, it was determined that a number of savings would not be deliverable within the financial year.

findings.headline: DSG deficit of £148.7m is draining £4.9m/year in foregone cash interest that could fund services
findings.detail: The Dedicated Schools Grant deficit, held separately from the General Fund due to statutory override, still creates a real financial issue by reducing available cash. The council has £148.7m less liquidity than it would otherwise. The High Needs Block continues to overspend substantially despite government intervention through the High Needs Stability Grant.
findings.matters: Lenders assess actual cash position and structural solvency, not accounting treatment. A £148.7m cash drain materially affects borrowing capacity and service funding capacity in future years.
findings.figures: £148.7m cumulative DSG deficit; £4.9m annual interest foregone; £1.3m projected shortfall in DSG recovery reserves by March 2028
findings.quote: whilst the deficit is therefore held separately from the General Fund, there is a cashflow pressure resulting from carrying a £148.7m deficit meaning that the Council has access to £148.7m less cash than it would otherwise. As a result, interest foregone on the deficit equates to £4.9m of pressure met by the General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: Lease disclosures contain £7.9m sampling error and multiple lease record inaccuracies, indicating asset and liability data quality issues.
findings.detail: Testing of the Council as Lessee note identified errors in rental values and lease terms. A £7.9m sampling error was identified but not corrected in the financial statements. Management attributes this to ongoing data cleansing work within Assets & Property as part of a 12-month improvement plan.
findings.matters: Lease record inaccuracies affect both asset valuations and liability calculations under IFRS 16; a £7.9m error that remains uncorrected suggests materiality thresholds may be set too high or data quality is systematically worse than assumed.
findings.figures: £7.9m unadjusted sampling error in lease disclosures
findings.quote: Testing identified that the lease information used to populate this note was not kept up to date resulting in the total unadjusted sampling error of £7.9 million.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: Property valuation program change created unexpected movements and one transposed-values error requiring the valuer to re-issue reports.
findings.detail: The council changed valuers and identified nine valuations with unexpected movements. One valuation error involved transposed values between the summary sheet and detailed calculations; management requested the valuer reissue reports. Auditors satisfied no material issue remains, but the incident flags valuation process weaknesses.
findings.matters: Valuation errors and process failures increase the risk of misstated asset bases, which feed into capital financing decisions and reserves calculations; a £496m asset base leaves little margin for error.
findings.figures: Total year-end valuation £496m (net increase £11m from 2023/24); nine valuations with unexpected movements
findings.quote: The change in the Authority's main valuer has resulted in a number of unexpected movements in valuations. We have also identified one instance where the values of land and buildings were transposed between the valuer's summary sheet and detailed calculations.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: IFRS 16 lease implementation revealed £4.4m in valuation errors and £14.4m in unrecorded peppercorn lease assets, indicating incomplete asset records.
findings.detail: Auditors identified errors in lease accounting on transition to IFRS 16: a £4.2m care home incorrectly recognized, a £3.7m school asset omitted from register, and a calculation error. Additionally, £14.4m of peppercorn lease assets (school buildings, land, buildings) were recognized for the first time, suggesting asset records were not previously complete.
findings.matters: Large unrecorded assets indicate gaps in the council's asset management and valuation processes; corrections of this magnitude suggest prior financial statements may have been similarly misstated.
findings.figures: £4.4m error in testing; £14.4m peppercorn lease asset increase; £3.7m school asset omitted
findings.quote: The Authority identified £8.6m of commercial leases. We identified three errors in our testing. These related to a care home (value £4.2m) which was incorrectly recognised when a under lease had been granted for the effective life of the lease. One asset was recognised in opening balances when it was acquired during the year.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: Council changed minimum revenue provision (MRP) policy to a less prudent basis, reducing the annual debt repayment charge by £3.7m (from £20.1m to £16.4m).
findings.detail: The council moved from charging 4% flat to a 40-year annuity basis for post-2008 capital spend. Auditors note this is 'less prudent than the Authority's previous approach' and results in a lower charge, though still compliant with guidance and approved by Full Council on 25 March 2025.
findings.matters: A less prudent MRP policy reduces current-year charges to revenue, improving short-term financial position at the cost of increased long-term debt burden; this signals financial pressure and reduces borrowing headroom.
findings.figures: MRP charge fell by £3.7m (20.2% reduction); new charge £16.4m represents 2.93% of capital financing requirement
findings.quote: The Authority has changed its approach for post-2008 capital financing requirement moving to a 40 year period on an annuity basis. The revised policy is less prudent than the Authority's previous approach and results in a lower charge.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: Multiple unadjusted misstatements totaling £6.3m remain in the financial statements, including pension fund valuations, lease assets, and PFI liabilities.
findings.detail: Auditors identified but management did not correct: £1.48m pension fund asset understatement, £4.4m overstatement of commercial lease assets, and £2.3m PFI liability overstatement. These remain in the published accounts.
findings.matters: Unadjusted errors indicate either immateriality or management choice not to correct them; their accumulation and nature suggest underlying accounting control weaknesses that could hide larger issues.
findings.figures: £1.48m pension asset understatement; £4.4m lease asset overstatement; £2.3m PFI liability overstatement
findings.quote: The audit of Dorset Pension Fund identified two understatement errors relating to the differences in asset valuations arising from timing differences due to the necessity to meet completion deadlines for the financial statements.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: Internal audit identified failures in procurement regulations, budget monitoring and contract management; police investigation ongoing as of 28 November 2025
findings.detail: An internal audit review uncovered control failures in the council's building compliance work. Police were still investigating as of 28 November 2025. Although auditors concluded the total spend was immaterial, the control environment failures are significant and apply to areas affecting financial reporting.
findings.matters: Procurement and budget monitoring failures expose the council to fraud risk, regulatory penalties, and potential project cost overruns; active police involvement signals reputational and legal risk.
findings.figures: Investigation scope was immaterial to financial statements, but control deficiencies spanned procurement, budget monitoring, and contract management
findings.quote: An investigation was undertaken during the audit period relating to works to ensure that the Council complied with building health and safety regulations. A review by the Council's internal auditors identified failures in procurement regulations, budget monitoring and contract management arrangements. We also met with Dorset Police on 28 November 2025 to obtain the latest update on progress and scope of their ongoing inquiries.

findings.paper_title: Appendix 1 - Audit Findings (ISA 260) Report for Dorset Council
findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit has risen to £95.63m with a £37.3m in-year overspend, identified as a significant weakness for the second consecutive year.
findings.detail: The DSG deficit is continuing to deteriorate rather than stabilize or improve. This was flagged as a significant weakness in 2023/24 and remains so for 2024/25. The scale of the annual overspend (£37.3m) indicates ongoing structural funding issues in education provision.
findings.matters: A growing unfunded education deficit signals unsustainable service delivery and limits the council's financial flexibility for other priorities; it is a key indicator of financial stress that lenders monitor closely.
findings.figures: £95.63m cumulative deficit; £37.3m in-year overspend
findings.quote: The Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) cumulative deficit rose to £95.63m, following an in year overspend of £37.3m. This was raised as a significant weakness in 2023/24 and given the continued deterioration in 2024/25 has remained a significant weakness this year.

findings.headline: Council is adopting a short-term borrowing strategy dependent on interest rates falling as forecast—introducing refinancing risk if rates remain higher than expected
findings.detail: The Council states in section 5.3 that it expects to use short-term borrowing or internal resources rather than long-term fixed-rate debt, because 'short-term interest rates are currently higher than in the recent past but are expected to fall in the coming year'. This is a deliberate tactical bet: avoid locking in high long-term rates now, but accept the risk of refinancing at potentially higher costs if interest rates do not fall as Arlingclose forecasts. The Council's Treasury adviser (Arlingclose) forecasts Bank Rate will fall to 3.25% by mid-2026; if that does not happen, near-term refinancing costs could be higher than budgeted.
findings.matters: This strategy depends on economic forecasts proving accurate. The economic outlook is uncertain (modest growth, rising unemployment, geopolitical risks noted in the Arlingclose forecast). If the forecast is wrong and rates remain elevated, the Council could face unexpected debt service cost increases that would require revenue cuts or further asset sales.
findings.figures: Bank Rate current 3.75%, forecast to 3.25%; average maturity of existing borrowing 20.1 years; average rate 4.5%
findings.quote: Short-term interest rates are currently higher than in the recent past but are expected to fall in the coming year and it is therefore likely to be more cost effective over the medium-term to either use internal resources, or to borrow short-term loans instead.

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to increase by 31% to £380m as the capital financing requirement grows to £509m
findings.detail: External borrowing is forecast to rise from £292m at December 2025 to £380m by March 2028, driven by an increasing capital financing requirement (CFR) that grows from £434m to £509m. The Council's liability benchmark—the minimum prudent level of external borrowing needed to fund its capital plans while maintaining minimum cash—is forecast to reach £375m by March 2028. All borrowing remains within prudential limits, but the trajectory shows increasing leverage.
findings.matters: Higher external debt means higher mandatory debt service costs that must be met from revenue, reducing flexibility for other spending. The Council is becoming more leveraged; any deterioration in its revenue position (from economic downturn, service failure, or loss of grant) would leave less room for adjustment.
findings.figures: External borrowing £292m (31-Dec-2025) to £380m (31-Mar-2028); CFR £434m to £509m
findings.quote: The 'gap' between the solid red line (liability benchmark) and the grey shaded areas (existing borrowing) indicates the minimum amount and duration of additional external borrowing the Council is forecast to need to fund the capital programme over the next twenty years.

findings.headline: Cash and investment balances forecast to decline to minimum prudent operating levels over the next four years
findings.detail: The Council's cash and investments are forecast to fall from £62m in March 2025 to £35m by March 2029, approaching the minimum threshold of £30m that the Council states is needed to maintain liquidity while minimising credit risk. This reflects a deliberate strategy to use internal resources ('internal borrowing') to fund the capital programme rather than taking on additional external debt. The Council will have minimal buffer above its own stated minimum.
findings.matters: Declining liquidity reduces the Council's financial flexibility to absorb unexpected shocks—service failures, capital project overruns, or revenue shortfalls—without forced borrowing on unfavourable terms. It also indicates growing reliance on external funding for stability.
findings.figures: Cash and investments: £62m (31-Mar-2025) to £45m (31-Mar-2026 forecast) to £35m (31-Mar-2029 budget); minimum operating threshold: £30m
findings.quote: cash and investment balances are kept to a minimum level of £30m at each year-end to maintain sufficient liquidity but minimise credit risk

findings.headline: S.151 Officer provides formal assurance that the capital programme is 'prudent, affordable and sustainable' despite rising debt burdens
findings.detail: At the close of the strategy, the Section 151 Officer (chief financial officer) has formally stated satisfaction with the sustainability of the proposed capital programme. This is the required statutory assurance under the Prudential Code, but it stands alongside the factual increases in debt, financing costs, and declining reserves documented in the strategy.
findings.matters: This is the officer's formal accountability statement for financial sustainability; the existence of this assurance alongside rising debt metrics suggests the council views the borrowing as manageable, but the assurance should be stress-tested against the actual numbers
findings.figures: Statement appears in section 4.5 (final paragraph)
findings.quote: The Section 151 Officer is satisfied that the proposed capital programme is prudent, affordable and sustainable.

findings.headline: Capital Financing Requirement (total borrowing need) rising 17% from £434m to £509m at peak, reflecting substantial capital programme commitments
findings.detail: The CFR measures the council's cumulative borrowing requirement for capital assets. The increase from £434m to £509m by 2028 indicates significant capital expenditure planned over the strategy period. The S.151 Officer has assessed this as prudent and sustainable, but the scale represents a material commitment of future revenue.
findings.matters: The rising CFR locks the council into higher debt service for years to come; a lender would want to understand whether the underlying capital programme is essential or discretionary, and whether the forecast benefits justify the cost
findings.figures: Capital Financing Requirement: £434m (2025 actual), £460m (2026), £494m (2027), £509m (2028), £494m (2029)
findings.quote: The Council's cumulative outstanding amount of debt finance is measured by the Capital Financing Requirement (CFR). This increases with new debt-financed capital expenditure and reduces with MRP and capital receipts used to replace debt.

findings.headline: Treasury investment reserves forecast to decline from £27m to £0m by 2029 while debt rises, reducing financial flexibility
findings.detail: The council's pooled treasury investments are being drawn down to zero by 2029 as part of its treasury strategy. Combined with stable cash holdings of £35m, total liquid resources decline from £63m (2025 actual) to £35m (2029 budget). This occurs while external borrowing is increasing, leaving less cushion for unexpected revenue pressures or opportunities.
findings.matters: A council depleting short-term investment reserves while increasing debt reduces its ability to absorb revenue shocks or fund essential spending without additional borrowing; signals tightening financial position
findings.figures: Treasury investments: £27m (2025 actual) → £10m (2026) → £5m (2027) → £0m (2028-29); Total cash and investments: £63m (2025) → £45m (2026) → £35m (2029)
findings.quote: Both near-term and longer-term investments may be held in pooled funds, where an external fund manager makes decisions on which particular investments to purchase, and the Council may request its money back at short notice.

findings.headline: Council plans to borrow above the 'lowest risk' liability benchmark throughout the medium term, with a gap of £32m in 2026 declining to £5m by 2029
findings.detail: The liability benchmark represents the minimum borrowing the council would need if it maintained only the minimum recommended cash reserves of £30m. The council's actual borrowing strategy sits above this benchmark, indicating it is holding less cash than the most conservative strategy would suggest. The gap narrows over time but remains material.
findings.matters: This is an explicit choice to accept a higher-risk financing position than the regulatory minimum-risk alternative; it signals either capital priorities requiring additional borrowing or a tolerance for reduced financial headroom
findings.figures: Liability benchmark (lowest risk): £260m (2025), £315m (2026), £350m (2027), £375m (2028), £365m (2029); Forecast borrowing above benchmark by: £32m (2026), £15m (2027), £10m (2028), £5m (2029)
findings.quote: The table below shows that the Council expects borrowing to be above its liability benchmark over the medium-term.

findings.headline: External borrowing forecast to rise from £330m in 2026 to peak at £380m in 2028, a 15% increase over the period
findings.detail: The council's gross debt is planned to increase substantially to finance the capital programme. Interest payable on borrowing rises from £16m to £17m per year and Minimum Revenue Provision (debt repayment) increases from £13m to £16m. Net financing costs rise from £21m to £31m, an increase of 48% in absolute terms.
findings.matters: Rising debt service costs reduce revenue flexibility and increase exposure to interest rate movements; a material drag on the council's revenue budget as these costs compound
findings.figures: External borrowing: £292m (2025 actual), £330m (2026 forecast), £360m (2027), £380m (2028), £370m (2029); Interest payable: £13m → £17m; MRP: £12m → £16m; Net financing costs: £21m (5.0% of revenue) → £31m (5.8%)
findings.quote: Projected levels of the Council's total outstanding debt which comprises borrowing, Private Finance Initiative (PFI) liabilities and leases are shown below and compared with the capital financing requirement.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet MTFP and budget report including appendices 1 - 6
findings.headline: S151 Officer assesses current financial risk as high, and residual risk remains high
findings.detail: The council's Chief Finance Officer (S151 Officer) has formally assessed the current risk level as high, and even after taking into account proposed mitigations, the residual risk remains high. The report explicitly states 'Readers of this report should therefore anticipate that achieving a balanced budget will likely require a reprioritisation of service delivery to maintain long-term financial sustainability.'
findings.matters: The S151 Officer is the statutory officer responsible for financial sustainability. A formal high-risk assessment is a warning that conventional budget balancing is approaching its limits.
findings.figures: Current Risk: High; Residual Risk: High
findings.quote: the acting S151 Officer, the Council's Chief Finance Officer, has assessed the current financial risk level as high. Readers of this report should therefore anticipate that achieving a balanced budget will likely require a reprioritisation of service delivery to maintain long-term financial sustainability.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet MTFP and budget report including appendices 1 - 6
findings.headline: Dorset receives among the lowest education funding per pupil nationally, £4,700 below the national average for high-needs pupils
findings.detail: Fair Funding Review 2.0 removed the 'remoteness' factor from all but Adult Social Care funding. Dorset, a rural council, is now funded as if it were less remote than it is. The council receives one of the lowest High Needs Block allocations per EHCP compared with statistical neighbours and roughly £4,700 less per high-needs pupil than the national average. This structural underfunding is driving the DSG deficit.
findings.matters: Dorset is legally required to fund education for all pupils with EHCPs, but the government is not funding it at the level of comparators or the national average. This is a structural deficit written into the formula, not a management problem.
findings.figures: £4,700 less per high-needs pupil than national average; among lowest High Needs Block per EHCP vs statistical neighbours
findings.quote: Dorset receives one of the lowest High Needs Block allocations per EHCP compared with our statistical neighbours, and roughly £4,700 less per high needs pupil than the national average.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet MTFP and budget report including appendices 1 - 6
findings.headline: 93% of the £25.9m CSP growth is dependent on Council Tax increases; CT rising from 69% to 73% of total resources
findings.detail: The government's Core Spending Power increase of £25.9m assumes councils will raise Council Tax to the maximum allowed (3% plus 2% social care precept). For Dorset, £24.1m of the £25.9m increase must come from Council Tax. Across the MTFP, Council Tax is growing from 69% to 73% of total funding, meaning the council is becoming ever more dependent on local taxation and less reliant on government funding.
findings.matters: Councils have limited power to raise Council Tax beyond the threshold—doing so requires a local referendum. Dorset is approaching the practical limit of what ratepayers can bear, leaving no buffer for future pressures.
findings.figures: CSP increase £25.9m; £24.1m (93%) from Council Tax; Council Tax dependency rising from 69% to 73%; total increase 4.9904%
findings.quote: Of this £25.9m, £24.1m (93%) is reliant upon the requirement to generate additional Council Tax revenue.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet MTFP and budget report including appendices 1 - 6
findings.headline: Business rates reduced by £15.2m (15% cut) in 2026/27 due to government reset
findings.detail: The government's business rates reset realigns funding nationally. Dorset's retained business rates fall from £73.1m in 2025/26 to £57.9m in 2026/27. Over the three-year MTFP, grant funding is also reducing by £6m. These are structural losses that cannot be recovered.
findings.matters: The council has lost a major income source through policy change, not through any action of its own. This compounds the pressure to raise Council Tax.
findings.figures: Business rates: £73.1m (2025/26) to £57.9m (2026/27), a loss of £15.2m; grants reducing £6m over 3 years
findings.quote: The reset of business rates sees the council's retained business rates reduced by around 15%.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet MTFP and budget report including appendices 1 - 6
findings.headline: 2025/26 forecast overspend of £4.4m requiring immediate use of reserves
findings.detail: The council is fully using its budgeted contingency in 2025/26 to cover a £4.4m overspend and is drawing on reserves to meet both this overspend and costs of the transformation programme. This reduces financial flexibility heading into a constrained MTFP period.
findings.matters: Reserves are already being depleted to cover current-year gaps. This indicates the council is operating beyond its sustainable funding level now, not just in future years.
findings.figures: £4.4m (1.05%) forecast overspend; contingency fully used; reserves drawn for transformation programme
findings.quote: The 2025/26 quarter 3 finance management report will be presented to Cabinet in January 2026 alongside this paper, providing the latest detail on the financial matters affecting the 2025/26 budget. Where service overspends cannot be mitigated, this will have a consequential impact on the financial position for 2026/27 and future years.

findings.paper_title: Cabinet MTFP and budget report including appendices 1 - 6
findings.headline: DSG cumulative deficit of £148.59m with statutory override ending March 2028, risking section 114 notice
findings.detail: The High Needs Block is forecasting a £54.279m overspend in 2025/26. The cumulative DSG deficit has reached £148.59m (£112.3m after partner contributions). The government's statutory override, which prevents this from hitting council reserves, ends in March 2028. The council explicitly states that without changes to funding or policy, it may face a section 114 notice at that point.
findings.matters: A section 114 notice is effectively insolvency; it means a council cannot legally spend money. This is an existential risk within two years unless SEND funding is reformed.
findings.figures: £148.59m cumulative deficit; £54.279m 2025/26 overspend; £5m annual servicing cost; override ends March 2028
findings.quote: Without changes to funding or policy this would mean that many councils - including Dorset – may have to face a section 114 notice when the statutory override ends in March 2028.

findings.headline: £27.5m of treasury investments held in volatile bond and property funds with acknowledged price risk
findings.detail: The council holds strategic pooled funds in bonds (£8.5m) and property (£19.0m), representing 77% of all treasury investments. The council acknowledges these will experience 'capital values will fluctuate over the short term.' These are longer-duration, higher-risk holdings aimed at returns above cash over 3-5 years.
findings.matters: Market downturns could generate material unrealised losses on the £27.5m portfolio, eroding the balance sheet precisely when the council faces reserve pressure. In a market stress scenario, the council may face simultaneous reserve depletion and balance sheet deterioration.
findings.figures: £27.5m in strategic pooled funds of £93.4m total investments (30 Sept 2025); breakdown: short-dated bond funds £2.9m, strategic bond funds £5.6m, property funds £19.0m
findings.quote: These investments are held for the longer term with the acceptance that capital values will fluctuate over the short term but with the expectation that over a three to five-year period total returns will exceed cash interest rates.

findings.headline: Council explicitly states it will have 'less reserves available to support internal borrowing' than at year start
findings.detail: The council is forced to increase external borrowing by £33m despite capital needs rising only £30m. This mismatch is directly attributed to reserve depletion. The council cannot finance capital spending from its own resources as it once did, requiring higher external debt to compensate.
findings.matters: Declining capacity for internal borrowing signals weakening financial position. As reserves shrink, the council becomes more dependent on external borrowing markets, reducing flexibility and raising debt servicing costs. This is a key indicator of reserve adequacy deterioration.
findings.figures: External borrowing forecast to increase £33m; CFR increase only £30m; £3m excess driven by reserve drawdown
findings.quote: External borrowing is forecast to increase by about £33m over the year, higher than the increase in CFR as the Council is expected to have less reserves available to support 'internal borrowing' than it did at the beginning of the year.

findings.headline: Cash and treasury investments forecast to fall from £93m (30 Sept 2025) to £35m (31 March 2026), £30m below £65m budget
findings.detail: The council held £93m in cash and treasury investments at 30 September but forecasts this will fall to £35m by 31 March 2026. This represents a £58m drawdown in the final six months and leaves the council £30m short of its planned reserve level. This is a material reduction in the council's liquidity buffer.
findings.matters: Rapid reserve depletion, particularly falling below budget, is a leading indicator of financial stress. It reduces the council's ability to absorb unexpected costs and signals either accelerated capital spend or cash consumption for operations. A lender needs assurance that reserve decline is planned and sustainable.
findings.figures: £93m mid-year (30 Sept 2025), forecast £35m at year-end (31 March 2026), vs budgeted £65m; decline of 62% from mid-year position
findings.quote: At 30 September 2025 the Council held cash and treasury investments of £93m compared to £63m at 31 March 2025 and is forecast to fall to £35m by 31 March 2026, compared to the budget of £65m.

findings.headline: Capital programme slipping: CFR growth only £30m against budget of £36m
findings.detail: Capital Financing Requirement forecast to rise to £465m by year-end, significantly less than the budgeted £470m. The document explicitly attributes this underspend to 'slippage in delivering the capital programme.' This indicates the council is not spending as much on capital as planned.
findings.matters: Capital programme delays signal delivery challenges or reprioritisation that may affect the council's asset base and medium-term borrowing requirements. A lender monitoring capital investment progress needs to understand whether slippage reflects temporary timing or structural delivery risk.
findings.figures: CFR forecast £465m vs budget £470m; implied capital slippage of approximately £6m
findings.quote: The CFR is forecast to rise by about £30m over the year to roughly £465m, less than budgeted due to slippage in delivering the capital programme.

findings.paper_title: Update on Response to SWAP Investigation for 24th November Audit and Governance
findings.headline: Council added medium-rated strategic risk to corporate register for control framework breaches
findings.detail: Dorset Council added risk 807/82 to its corporate risk register, acknowledging that breaches in the oversight and control framework could result in future unauthorized approvals and financial mismanagement. The risk is rated medium currently and is expected to remain at medium pending completion of wider organizational learning actions.
findings.matters: The council's own risk assessment indicates the governance failures could recur, and signals that residual control risk remains elevated until further progress is demonstrated
findings.figures: Risk 807/82; Current and Residual ratings both MEDIUM
findings.quote: Due to a breach in the oversight and control framework, contract and expenditure approvals may breach constitutional requirements, resulting in overspends and financial mismanagement.

findings.paper_title: Update on Response to SWAP Investigation for 24th November Audit and Governance
findings.headline: SWAP investigation findings remain incomplete, with 34 remedial actions still being validated and assigned
findings.detail: While the compliance audit actions are substantially complete (16 of 18), the investigation into what actually occurred is still in process. The 34 actions arising from the SWAP investigation remain under validation and assignment to senior officers. Actions will only be formally tracked once finalized with SWAP.
findings.matters: The full scope, severity, and remediation timeline for the governance failures remain unknown; this incompleteness means the council's exposure is not yet quantified
findings.figures: 34 investigation actions pending; 16 of 18 audit actions complete or in progress
findings.quote: there is an ongoing process to validate, assign senior officers, agree priority and remove duplicate actions working closely with SWAP.

findings.paper_title: Update on Response to SWAP Investigation for 24th November Audit and Governance
findings.headline: Procurement system allowed impersonation and approvals breaching delegated thresholds for nearly two years undetected
findings.detail: The Comensura procurement system permitted users to hold dual roles, enabling impersonation without audit trails. Simultaneously, authorization levels in the finance system did not align with the Scheme of Delegation, allowing transactions to be approved that breached delegated spending thresholds. These failures persisted from December 2022 through October 2024.
findings.matters: Control system failures enabled unauthorized spending approvals to proceed without detection for an extended period, indicating material weaknesses in the council's financial oversight framework
findings.figures: Period: December 2022 to October 2024; system controls fixed December 2024
findings.quote: User permissions in c.net allowed people to have more than one role and act as someone else, without proper records. Transactions in c.net were approved incorrectly, breaking the rules for who can approve what.

news_drafts.headline: Dorset Council expects £145m high needs grant in November; schools deficit was £148.7m in March
news_drafts.lead:
Dorset Council expects a £145m High Needs Stability Grant from government in November, after its Reform Plan for special educational needs and disabilities (SEND) was accepted in October 2026. Its cumulative deficit on the dedicated schools grant, the government grant that funds schools, was £148.7m at 31 March 2026. The grant is forecast to overspend by £74.3m in 2026/27.

The Cabinet finance report calls acceptance of the plan a key milestone in securing a 90% write-off of the cumulative overspend. The £145m leaves a balance of £3.7m, to be funded from the reserve set up to support the Safety Valve programme. The medium-term financial plan report says the projections show the deficit returning to around £150m at 31 March 2028, when the statutory override, the government rule that keeps the deficit off the council's main balance sheet, ceases. The finance report says the override was extended from March 2026 to March 2028, and puts the carrying cost of the deficit at circa £6m in interest foregone.

The same report forecasts SEND transport spending at £22.3m for 2026/27, up 10% from £20.2m in 2025/26. It says 2025/26 had the lowest increase in recent history, which it attributes to market stability and efficiency work by Dorset Travel. Contract changes from September 2026 have been assessed as circa £2.2m below budget for SEND transport and circa £0.5m below budget for mainstream school transport.

news_drafts.headline: Dorset Council forecasts a £74.3m schools grant overspend for 2026/27, within high needs
news_drafts.lead:
Dorset Council forecasts a £74.315m overspend on its dedicated schools grant (DSG), the government grant that funds schools, for 2026/27, according to papers for the Schools' Forum meeting on 6 November. The forecast, made at 30 September 2026, sits in the high needs block, the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND). The council budgeted for an in-year deficit of £73.328m.

The paper attributes the main pressure to growth in SEND demand and in the number of children with an education, health and care plan. The cumulative deficit was £148.7m at 31 March 2026. The council expects a £145m High Needs Stability Grant in November 2026, after its SEND Reform Plan was accepted in October, which brings the forecast cumulative deficit at March 2027 to £76.719m. The deficit is forecast at about £150m by 31 March 2028. The paper says the council has access to £148.7m less cash than it would otherwise, at a cost of circa £6m in interest foregone. A statutory override, a temporary government rule that keeps the deficit off the council's main balance sheet, was extended from March 2026 to March 2028 in June 2025.

The forum also has a plan to commission 2,056 specialist places for September 2027, committing £17.9m of the high needs block: 996 in special schools, 397 in learning centres, 370 in further education colleges and 293 in Specialist Inclusion Bases. The paper says this will be funded from the block in 2027-28 and 2028-29.

news_drafts.headline: Dorset Council's risk register rates schools high needs funding instability "High", unchanged since Quarter 4
news_drafts.lead:
Dorset Council's Audit and Governance Committee, meeting on 12 October 2026, has before it a risk register entry rating as "High" the possibility that instability in the high needs budget could push the council into deficit. High needs is the part of school funding for children with special educational needs and disabilities. The rating is unchanged from Quarter 4.

The entry, numbered Risk 194, says that "Instability in the High Needs Block budget may create an increased deficit in the Dedicated Schools Grant (DSG) resulting in a deficit in Dorset Councils financial position." The dedicated schools grant is the government grant that funds schools. A deficit on it would be an overspend, usually on support for children with special needs. The papers give no figures for the size of the deficit or the budget.

The same issue appears in the committee's action list. A previous report identified the instability as a significant matter and asked for reassurance from the Cabinet Member for Education and Finance. The action is recorded as in progress, with no completion date. The tracker says the instability "may create increased deficit in the dedicated school grant resulting in deficit in Dorset Council's financial position".
